summary.text: Luminosity is the total amount of electromagnetic energy a star or other object gives off per unit of time, measured in watts.
It is not the same as apparent brightness, which also depends on how far away the object is and on any light absorbed on the way.
A star's luminosity can be worked out from two characteristics, its size and its effective temperature.

facts.label: Sun as a unit
facts.value: The Sun's luminosity is often used as a unit

facts.label: Neutrino share
facts.value: Neutrinos carry off about 2% of the Sun's energy

facts.label: Temperature link
facts.value: Proportional to temperature to the fourth power

facts.label: Most luminous stars
facts.value: Always young, no more than a few million years old

items.prompt: Two stars radiate exactly the same total power, but one is far more distant from you. Which quantity will differ as you observe them?

options.label: Their luminosity
Their apparent brightness
Their total energy output
Their radiant power

items.explain: Luminosity is the star's own output, while apparent brightness also depends on distance.

items.prompt: Class O stars are far hotter than class M stars. What does that gap do to how much energy they give off?

options.label: It makes almost no difference to their output
It makes their output differ by about the same ratio
It makes the cooler stars give off more
It makes their output differ by an even bigger ratio

items.explain: Luminosity is proportional to temperature to the fourth power, so a large temperature variation produces an even vaster luminosity variation.

items.prompt: A star is extremely massive and very luminous. What should you expect about how long it lasts?

options.label: A much shorter life than less massive stars
A much longer life than less massive stars
About the same life as less massive stars
A life that depends only on its distance

items.explain: Luminosity depends on a high power of mass, so high-mass luminous stars have much shorter lifetimes.

items.prompt: On Earth, a bolometer can measure total radiant energy directly. Why do astronomers build a mathematical model of a star's spectrum instead?

options.label: Bolometers only work in total darkness
Stars give off no energy a bolometer could absorb
Bolometers are not sensitive enough across the spectrum
Models are cheaper than any instrument

items.explain: Bolometers cannot measure a star's brightness because they are insufficiently sensitive across the electromagnetic spectrum, so astronomers measure at some wavelengths and model the rest.

items.prompt: Two stars have the same temperature, but one is more luminous. What does that tell you about the more luminous one?

options.label: It must be much younger
It must be much closer to us
It must be much less massive
It must be larger

items.explain: Increased luminosity at the same temperature indicates a larger star, which is why such stars are called giants or supergiants.

items.prompt: To work out how much energy a star radiates, an astronomer needs which two characteristics of it?

options.label: Its size and its effective temperature
Its age and its mass
Its colour and its name
Its position and its spin

items.explain: A star's luminosity can be determined from its size and its effective temperature.
